item.title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
item.dc:creator: Kyungtae Kim
June-Young M. Lee
Hyeongseop Kim
H.-S. Sim
item.description:
Authors: Kyungtae Kim, June-Young M. Lee, Hyeongseop Kim, H.-S. Sim
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Majorana bound states (MBSs) are zero-energy localized states in topological superconductors, obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. Manipulation of mobile MBSs, encompassing their on-demand generation, propagation, and fusion, is essential for braiding MBSs and operating topological qubits. We show that the manipulation is enabled by a trijunction formed on a topological insulator in a perpendicular magnetic field, where three Josephson junctions meet. While the superconducting phases at the trijunction center evolve to cross a boundary between topological and non-topological phase domains, the trijunction offers two distinct dynamics, source/sink and path, depending on the phase boundaries. At a source/sink boundary, two MBSs are pairwise generated at the center, and one of them is ejected to a Josephson junction. The reverse, pair annihilation by collision of two MBSs, can also happen. At a path boundary, an MBS moves from a Josephson junction to the trijunction center or vice versa, without involving other MBSs. Exploiting the two dynamics, fusion and braiding of MBSs can be operated in a trijunction network. We illustrate this with a double trijunction setup, where non-Abelian state evolutions associated with MBSs can be manipulated without dynamical control of the setup and detected by Josephson emission spectroscopy.

item.title: Mapping Future Energy Journeys Through Modeling the Global Transport of Synthetic Energy Carriers
item.dc:creator: Uwe Langenmayr
Julia Schuler
Viktor Slednev
Wolf Fichtner
item.description:
Authors: Uwe Langenmayr, Julia Schuler, Viktor Slednev, Wolf Fichtner
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11500
Abstract: Abstract Synthetic energy carriers can connect renewable-energy-rich potential production regions with distant demand centers, but the emergence of trade depends on total supply costs. Here, we develop a spatially resolved heuristic combining hydrogen production costs with ports, pipelines, and shipping routes, as well as syntheses, cracking, and reformation processes, to identify key import corridors. Across 10,883 production locations and seven different scenarios, we find that export regions connected to the importer through retrofit-ready pipelines remain competitive despite only moderate renewable potentials. Meanwhile, for remote exporters competitiveness depends on port availability and coastal access through pipeline networks. Gaseous hydrogen dominates short pipeline routes, and ammonia is preferred for maritime trade, whereas methanol and methane emerge in long multimodal chains. Additional results show that low-cost heat availability is required for the competitiveness of liquid organic hydrogen carriers, while accounting for market values of conventional counterparts boosts ammonia and methanol trade.

item.title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
item.dc:creator: Maya Bruderer
Jiangning Li
Andreas Kaczmarczyk
Simon van Vliet
Kai Schleicher
Rao Rohan Girish
Pablo Manfredi
Nicole Thürkauf
item.description:
Authors: Maya Bruderer, Jiangning Li, Andreas Kaczmarczyk, Simon van Vliet, Kai Schleicher, Rao Rohan Girish, Pablo Manfredi, Nicole Thürkauf, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Efficient colonisation of host tissue surfaces is a prerequisite for bacterial infection. In the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence, but how these pathways are coordinated during tissue infection has remained unclear. Here we demonstrate that cAMP and c-di-GMP establish mutually exclusive signalling states at the single-cell level, generating distinct subpopulations of motile and surface-attached cells through pathway-specific control of type IV pili (T4P). Initial surface contact triggers an increase in c-di-GMP, activating FimW and driving stable attachment via bipolar T4P formation. This state is progressively replaced by cAMP, which inactivates FimW-dependent attachment and induces FimX-mediated T4P polarisation, surface motility and virulence activation. The resulting signalling transition enforces coexisting subpopulations, with attached cells gradually displaced by spreading cells. Using a human airway tissue model, we show that both T4P-mediated adhesion and twitching motility are required for invasion and tissue damage. Based on this, we propose that reciprocal cAMP–c-di-GMP signalling coordinates complementary T4P functions to optimise P. aeruginosa surface colonisation and infection.

item.title: Insular motor and error encoding supports self-correcting intracranial brain-computer interface
item.dc:creator: Paul Weger
Sophia Gimple
Maarten C. Ottenhoff
Maxime Verwoert

Albert Colon

item.description:
Authors: Paul Weger, Sophia Gimple, Maarten C. Ottenhoff, Maxime Verwoert, Lauren Ostrowski, Albert Colon, Louis Wagner, Johannes P. van Dijk, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Error recognition is fundamental to adaptive behavior, enabling rapid compensatory action when outcomes deviate from expectations. Central to this function are neural circuits for performance monitoring, encoding cognitive signals that could support more reliable neural interfaces. Here, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in epilepsy patients to enable a motor brain-computer interface (BCI) while sampling error-related activity across a distributed network. Our work reveals high-frequency population dynamics emerging in the anterior insula and propagating to the prefrontal cortex as the interface fails to follow the user’s intention. We identify spatially organized insular responses to error processing and movement feedback, highlighting it as a heterogeneous hub linking action and outcome. Frontoinsular recording sites were found to preferentially encode error-related activity, while centroparietal responses were intermixed with compensatory motor signals, making the former a compelling target for real-time error correction. Together, our findings demonstrate a human intracranial BCI harnessing insular brain activity, integrating cognitive processes directly into device control.

item.title: Addressing the 1000-h/1000-nit stability challenge in perovskite LEDs
item.dc:creator: Yucai Yuan
Shiyu Xing
Gan Zhang
Bo Li
Suhui Zhang
Shengnan Liu
Yu Pan
Zhuoyue Gu
item.description:
Authors: Yucai Yuan, Shiyu Xing, Gan Zhang, Bo Li, Suhui Zhang, Shengnan Liu, Yu Pan, Zhuoyue Gu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) offer exceptional colour purity and efficiency for next-generation display applications. Despite the recent advances in device stability, achieving long-term stable PeLEDs under display-relevant conditions remains a critical challenge. The actual device half-life (T 50 ) experimentally measured for visible PeLEDs were in most cases limited to below 1000 h for any given brightness, in contrast to the much longer extrapolated lifetimes reported. Here, we demonstrate stable green PeLEDs with a T 50 lifetime of 1350 h at an initial luminance of 1000 cd m −2 (nits), a maximum energy-conversion efficiency of 28.0%, and a peak external quantum efficiency of 24.5%. The exceptional performance is enabled by the insertion of a fluorinated self-assembled monolayer between the metal oxide and polymeric hole-transport layers. This molecular interlayer leads to Ohmic-like characteristics for charge injection, lowering the operating voltage at ~1000 nits to sub-bandgap levels (~2.1 V) where ion migration is suppressed. The accumulated photon output of our PeLEDs over the course of their T 50 lifespan is found to sharply increase as the driving voltage drops to sub-bandgap values, highlighting the critical role of employing low-voltage device architectures in reaching the 1350-h/1000-nit stability milestone. Finally, a flexible active-matrix PeLED display prototype is developed, showing the potential of the devices for wearable optoelectronics.

item.title: [18F]FET PET enables histopathology-validated detection of non-contrast-enhancing glioblastoma
item.dc:creator: R. Stürzl
S. V. Kirchleitner
J. Lorenz
K. J. Schmidbauer
V. Stöcklein
S. Quach

item.description:
Authors: R. Stürzl, S. V. Kirchleitner, J. Lorenz, K. J. Schmidbauer, V. Stöcklein, S. Quach, L. Kaiser, S. Stöcklein, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11498
Abstract: Abstract Accurate visualization of glioblastoma is essential for guiding biopsy, resection and radiotherapy. Contrast-enhanced MRI is routine in clinical practice, yet it can miss metabolically active tumor outside areas of blood-brain barrier disruption. In a histopathology-validated cohort with 472 tissue samples of 61 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, we show that O-(2-[¹⁸F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET ([ 18 F]FET PET) depicts tumor tissue significantly better than contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI), especially in regions that show no enhancement on MRI. [ 18 F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [ 18 F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management.

item.title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks
item.dc:creator: Mark Blümel
Andreas C. Schneider
Valentin Neuhaus
David A. Ehrlich
Marcel Graetz
Michael Wibral
Abdullah Makkeh
Viola Priesemann
item.description:
Authors: Mark Blümel, Andreas C. Schneider, Valentin Neuhaus, David A. Ehrlich, Marcel Graetz, Michael Wibral, Abdullah Makkeh, Viola Priesemann
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11499
Abstract: Abstract Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

item.title: A topographic video model predicts the spatio-functional organization of the human visual system
item.dc:creator: Yingtian Tang
Yash Shah
Florian Kolly
Daniel L. K. Yamins
Martin Schrimpf
item.description:
Authors: Yingtian Tang, Yash Shah, Florian Kolly, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Martin Schrimpf
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Taken together, we provide a computational framework for understanding the spatial and functional organization of high-level visual cortex.

item.title: Phospholipase D1 activates NAD kinase fuelling neutrophil extracellular trap formation
item.dc:creator: Rahaf Albarghash
Sergio G. San-Miguel
Arturo Zychlinsky
Dhiren Ferise Patel
item.description:
Authors: Rahaf Albarghash, Sergio G. San-Miguel, Arturo Zychlinsky, Dhiren Ferise Patel
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11497
Abstract: Abstract Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function.

item.dc:creator: Stanley Bram
Diego J. Orea

Soyu Zi

item.description:
Authors: Stanley Bram, Diego J. Orea, Graeme Lindsey, Soyu Zi, Jordan Quenneville, Hui Xu, Sarah Leach, Jenna J. Guthmiller, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

item.title: Bistable origami robot for adaptive multimodal motion actuated by nonuniform magnetic fields
item.dc:creator: Chong Huang
Zhuangzhi Miao
Sida Ma
Zheguo Tang
Heming Wang
Zhanpeng Cui
Yihao Fu
Yang Li
item.description:
Authors: Chong Huang, Zhuangzhi Miao, Sida Ma, Zheguo Tang, Heming Wang, Zhanpeng Cui, Yihao Fu, Yang Li
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Conventional magnetically controlled mini-robots require operation within highly uniform and high-precision magnetic fields, which are impractical for large space applications. In this work, the bistable origami robot offloads these requirements onto the pre-programmed geometry of its mechanical architecture. These structures exhibit distinct deformation modes at each stable state when subjected to small-amplitude magnetic perturbations. Moreover, transitions between stable states—triggered by large-amplitude impulsive magnetic inputs—enable impulsive motions such as grasping. Correspondingly, a large-workspace magnetic actuation system is developed to generate low-uniform magnetic fields, and it is capable of controlling the bistable origami structure for desired multimodal locomotion and manipulation. We demonstrate capabilities including self-grasping, object capture, and adaptive locomotion modes such as crawling, turning, tumbling, scampering, jumping, and rolling at two different stable configurations. Our findings offer an approach for designing multi-functional and wireless mini/microrobots in large spaces, which is validated through analytical modeling, numerical simulation, and experimental testing.

item.title: Estimating the resilience of non-stationary systems
item.dc:creator: Taylor Smith
Andreas Morr
Christof Schötz
Niklas Boers
item.description:
Authors: Taylor Smith, Andreas Morr, Christof Schötz, Niklas Boers
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11286
Abstract: Abstract A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

item.title: Photoredox cobalt-catalyzed late-stage N-methyl-selective C–H vinylation of unactivated trialkylamines with alkynes
item.dc:creator: Ze-Kai Shen
Ruihua Zhao
Yang Wu
Meng-Wei Zhu
Ji-Bao Xia
item.description:
Authors: Ze-Kai Shen, Ruihua Zhao, Yang Wu, Meng-Wei Zhu, Ji-Bao Xia
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here we show a photoredox/cobalt dual-catalytic strategy for N-methyl-selective α-C–H vinylation of unactivated tertiary alkylamines with internal alkynes. This redox-neutral method provides trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or external oxidants, with broad substrate scope and high regioselectivity, stereoselectivity and site-selectivity under mild conditions. The reaction accommodates diverse amines and alkynes, including electronically unbiased dialkyl alkynes, and enables gram-scale synthesis, preparation of the fungicide fenpropidin and late-stage functionalization of structurally complex pharmaceuticals. Some drug analogues show enhanced apparent human histamine H1 receptor binding affinity. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies support a reasonable reaction pathway involving α-amino carbon radical generation via photoredox catalysis, followed by aminomethyl-cobalt I -mediated alkyne migratory insertion and protonolysis. This work provides a practical strategy for selective trialkylamines editing and late-stage diversification.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The role of phonons in cuprates remains controversial, with their complex lattice structure complicating the investigation. Here, we identify phonon modes originating from charge reservoir and superconducting layers of Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ using sub-unit-cell resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy in a scanning transmission electron microscope. We reveal several phonon modes exhibiting layer-specific localization: ~78 meV in-plane modes localized in the CuO 2 planes, ~42 meV hybrid (in-plane and out-of-plane) modes in the CuO 2 planes, and ~38 meV hybrid modes in the BiO layers. We also observe a periodic modulation of phonon frequencies induced by the superstructure, spatially correlating with the superconducting gap variation. Our findings offer new insights into the lattice dynamics in cuprates, fostering deeper exploration of the microscopic linkage between structural modulation, electronic inhomogeneity, and electron-phonon coupling.

item.title: Hippocampal transformations occur along dimensions of memory interference
item.dc:creator: Soroush Mirjalili

item.description:
Authors: Soroush Mirjalili, Guo Wanjia, Dominik Grätz, Eric Z. Wang, Ulrich Mayr, Brice A. Kuhl
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference.

Authors: Xiaolei Wang, Zihe Wang, Haibo Qu, Peiyi Wang, Sheng Guo, Jinkyu Yang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Modern mechanical computing, being envisioned as a pathway toward structure- and material-level processing, holds potential for intelligent metamaterials and robotics in extreme environments. However, current computing architectures remain constrained by binary paradigms. Here, we introduce an origami-inspired modular architecture that encodes logical mappings into its inherent kinematic responses under an input-output decoupled paradigm, enabling both binary and ternary mechanical computing. Within this emerging paradigm, the multi-stable states of two Kresling origami configurations serve as physical carriers for generating discrete signals, while torsional transitions among these states ensure signal switching, supporting operations from logic gates to advanced arithmetic. Based on this mechanical architecture, we systematically demonstrate seven common logic gates and modular arithmetic half- and full-adders in both binary and ternary systems, revealing challenges and opportunities in advancing multi-valued logic through comparative analysis. The physical platform, along with its accompanying response-programming strategy, represents a simplified and generalized paradigm that supports migration to higher-level mechanical computing mechanisms.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11456
Abstract: Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

item.dc:creator: Arthur Prat-Carrabin

item.description:
Authors: Arthur Prat-Carrabin, Gilles de Hollander, Saurabh Bedi, Samuel J. Gershman, Christian C. Ruff
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The brain’s representations are encoded in the collective activity of neural populations whose non-monotonic tuning properties define the population code. Adaptive behavior calls for flexible retuning of this code as stimulus statistics change across contexts. Yet how such adaptation occurs is unknown. Using fMRI during a numerosity-estimation task with variable number ranges, we show that number representations in human parietal cortex dynamically recalibrate to context, enabling context-sensitive behavioral accuracy. The tuning properties of neural populations collectively shift and rescale with the range. This distributed range adaptation achieves efficient coding in real time: neural precision scales with the range and predicts corresponding changes in behavioral precision. Individuals with stronger neural adaptation show larger behavioral adjustments. These findings extend static sensory efficient coding to adaptive representations of abstract magnitudes. Such flexible population tuning may constitute a canonical mechanism of encoding networks that enables the brain to sustain precise, adaptive behavior.

Authors: L. H. A. Berman, D. Campbell, E. Hartmann, T. Heinemann, T. Wilson, B. Hidding, A. F. Habib
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract X-ray free-electron lasers are large and complex machines, limited by electron beam brightness. Here we show through start-to-end simulations how to realise compact, robust and tunable X-ray lasers in the water window, based on ultra-bright electron beams from plasma wakefield accelerators. First, an ultra-low-emittance electron beam is released by a plasma photocathode in a metre-scale plasma wakefield accelerator. By tuning the beam charge, space-charge forces create a balance between beam fields and wakefields that reduces beam energy spread and improves energy stability – both critical for beam extraction, transport, and focusing into a metre-scale undulator. Here, the resulting ultra-bright beams produce wavelength-tunable, coherent, femtosecond-scale photon pulses at strong gain. This regime enables reliable generation of multi-gigawatt-class X-ray laser pulses across the water window, offering tunability via the witness beam charge and robustness against variations in plasma wakefield strength and plasma photocathode laser jitter. Our findings help democratise access to coherent, high-power, soft X-ray radiation.

Authors: Hyewon Yun, Gwangsu Bak, Hyun Dong Jung, Jeongjin Kim, Hyunseo Dho, Seoin Back, Yun Jeong Hwang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Industrial flue gases typically contain only 3–15% CO 2 , and direct electrochemical reduction on such dilute feeds would eliminate costly upstream purification. However, mass transport limitations and competing hydrogen evolution severely restrict activity under these CO 2 -starved conditions, and the governing molecular factors remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that pyridinic-nitrogen enrichment in Ni–N–C single-atom catalysts enables efficient CO 2 reduction under dilute CO 2 . By tuning the pyridinic-N to pyrrolic-N ratio in well-defined Ni–N x sites, we probe the role of local nitrogen environments in CO 2 reduction rather than the metal center alone. Electronic-state analysis and density functional theory reveal that pyridinic-N forms a reversible CO 2 adduct that enhances local CO 2 accessibility near the active Ni center through a desorption–re-adsorption relay. These findings provide molecular-level insight by identifying a neighboring motif that regulates local CO 2 availability without perturbing the intrinsic Ni–N reaction pathway, and by establishing a transferable design principle for CO 2 reduction catalysts under CO 2 -limited conditions.

Abstract: Abstract Differentiating arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency from primary polydipsia is challenging. The most accurate test, hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin, requires intensive monitoring. Intravenous mannitol stimulates AVP release and may provide a simpler alternative. In a randomized double-blind crossover trial, 22 healthy adults received mannitol and placebo in random order, of whom 21 were included in the primary analysis. In a pilot study, 10 patients with AVP deficiency and 10 with primary polydipsia received mannitol. The primary outcome was copeptin after mannitol infusion. Mannitol resulted in a 2.29-fold higher copeptin at 90 minutes (+6.4 pmol/L (95% CI: +5.2, +7.7; p <0.001)) than after placebo at mean baseline copeptin levels in healthy adults. In patients, copeptin after 30 minutes was 11.7 pmol/L (95% CI: 6.5, 17.0) higher in primary polydipsia than in AVP deficiency. Mannitol infusion shows promise as a new diagnostic approach. Larger confirmatory studies are required to validate both the optimal diagnostic cut-off and patient safety. Trial Registration number: NCT06542198 .

Abstract: Abstract Atypical chemokine receptors (ACKRs) are non-signaling GPCRs that regulate ligand availability, with ACKR3 functioning as a dual scavenger of chemokines and opioid peptides. In contrast, basal EV release is governed by intracellular sorting processes and influenced by receptor ubiquitination and RAMP3. We also show that the release on EVs, in particular under basal conditions, is observed for other receptors such as KOR, CXCR4 and several ACKRs. Collectively, these findings establish EVs as regulators in chemokine and opioid systems and as a distinct dimension of ACKR3 and more broadly GPCR biology.

Authors: Jingwen Weng, Xinlei Gao, Carlos Garcia, Ruihe Li, Kevin Gering, Wyatt Pena, Yong Yang, Ifan E. L. Stephens, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Electrolyte-dependent lifetime variability remains a major obstacle to sustainable deployment of lithium-ion batteries, contributing to premature retirement, increased material demand and uncertainty in lifecycle assessment. However, most continuum degradation models represent the electrolyte through bulk transport, without capturing its role in interfacial degradation. Here, we use customised multi-layer pouch cells with varied ethylene carbonate:dimethyl carbonate ratio, lithium hexafluorophosphate concentration and electrolyte amount to examine how electrolyte conditions shape degradation trajectories under accelerated degradation. Electrochemical diagnostics, gas analysis and post-mortem interfacial characterisation show that this divergence is associated with electrolyte-sensitive interphase growth, parasitic reactions and spatially heterogeneous surface degradation. We incorporate electrolyte-dependent transport and thermodynamic properties into a physics-based degradation model. A transport-only implementation does not reproduce the observed separation in capacity-retention trajectories. Introducing a minimal electrolyte-sensitive refinement through an effective interphase transport parameter improves agreement in the ethylene-carbonate-rich case. These results identify electrolyte-sensitive interfacial degradation as a necessary modelling dimension for reliable lifetime prediction.

item.description:
Authors: Anna-Lisa Schuler, Andrea Bruera, Gesa Hartwigsen
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11454
Abstract: Abstract Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus—a core lexico-semantic region—was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain’s capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

Abstract: Abstract Lipid metabolism is fundamental to cellular homeostasis, supporting energy storage, membrane architecture, and cellular signaling. Beyond these canonical roles, lipids have emerged as critical regulators of host immunity. Here, we define a lipid-driven mechanism that governs host–pathogen interactions by impacting pathogen clearance and thus infection outcomes. Exploiting Drosophila , we show that enteric infection triggers robust accumulation of neutral lipids, and specifically 1,2-diacylglycerols (DAGs), in the midgut. Disruption of DAG biosynthesis or lipid transport in midgut enterocytes (ECs) impairs lipid accumulation and reduces host survival. Conversely, dietary lipid supplementation enhances lipid storage and improves survival. Mechanistically, these lipid-dependent responses regulate defecation, thereby controlling bacterial clearance from the midgut. DAGs can act as signaling lipids that activate protein kinase C (PKC), and DAG accumulation in ECs correlates with elevated PKC activity and calcium signaling in midgut visceral muscle (VM), promoting VM contraction, midgut motility, and expulsion of pathogens via defecation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for DAG metabolism in shaping host defenses.

Abstract: Abstract Effective stress coping relies on neural and endocrine coordination, with the mesostriatal system serving as a central substrate. Here, we show dissociable roles of the nucleus accumbens (NAC) and dorsal caudate (dCA) and their associated brain networks in shaping stress responses. We identify neural stability (NS)—capturing stress-induced changes in state-switching frequency over the course of stress responses—as a marker: task-state NS correlates positively with stress-related NAC activity, whereas resting-state NS correlates inversely with stress-related dCA activity. NAC-mediated networks and associated NS further predict faster cortisol recovery. Intriguingly, NAC-related functional connectivity patterns spatially covary with dopamine D 2 receptor distributions and gene expression in inhibitory neurons and glia, whereas dCA-related patterns covary with μ-opioid receptor distributions. Together, these findings reveal striatal subregional heterogeneity in stress coping and characterize resilience as a multisystem homeostatic process integrating neural, endocrine, and molecular layers.

Abstract: Abstract Achieving high mechanical strength and environmental stability is critical for hydrogels in demanding engineering scenarios. Crystalline hydrogels hold promise because their crystallites act as physical crosslinks and energy dissipators; however, precise control over crystalline architecture remains underexplored. Inspired by industrial thermoplastic processing, we report an ASGS strategy for crystalline hydrogels that integrates alkali-induced chain activation (A), ultra-stretching-driven orientation (S), and glycerol-seawater-mediated densification (GS). Ultra-stretching establishes a highly oriented chain network, and subsequent densification achieves maximum crystallinity and highly oriented crystallites. This thermoplastic-inspired crystallization engineering provides a scalable paradigm for fabricating strong and stable crystalline hydrogels, promising for load-bearing and harsh underwater engineering applications.

Abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic urea synthesis from carbon dioxide and nitrate under ambient conditions offers a sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive Bosch-Meiser process. Abstract: Abstract How transcriptional asymmetry arises in the epiblast before gastrulation remains a central question in mammalian development. Using a targeted CRISPRa screen, we identify Wt1 as a regulator of lineage-associated transcriptional programmes during formative pluripotency. Guang-Chuan Xu

item.description:
Authors: Qian-Kun Fan, Guang-Chuan Xu, He Ma, Chuan-Kai Yu, Bo-Yang Sun, Gang He, Gong Chen, Hao Wang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer has emerged as a powerful strategy for alkene functionalization, yet its application to sterically congested tetrasubstituted alkenes remains severely underdeveloped. Here, we report an Ir(III)-catalyzed nitrene-triggered aziridination–rearrangement cascade that enables the efficient conversion of cyclic-substituted tetrasubstituted alkenes into cycloalkane-fused δ-lactams. The transformation proceeds under mild conditions with excellent yields and uniformly high diastereoselectivities and exhibits broad compatibility with carbon-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-based nucleophiles, including structurally complex and biologically relevant substrates. Combined experimental and computational studies support a concerted aziridination by an Ir–nitrenoid to generate a strained tricyclic intermediate, which undergoes a strain-release-driven aza-semipinacol rearrangement to furnish a bicyclic azacarbocation. Divergent nucleophilic interception or elimination of this intermediate provides rapid access to structurally diverse fused δ-lactam architectures. These findings establish a nitrene-triggered carbocationic rearrangement manifold for the functionalization of tetrasubstituted alkenes and expand the synthetic potential of transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer.
